Here’s a simpler breakdown of the article:

Ford recently announced it’s cutting 800 jobs in the UK and is now complaining about rules that require car companies to sell more electric vehicles (EVs) every year. They call these rules "unworkable," even though back in 2022, Ford was part of a **group** pushing for even stricter targets. They argued that lower **figures** wouldn’t send a strong enough message to buyers or investors. At the time, Ford believed the rules would help grow the EV market, but now they say the slowdown in demand has caught them off guard. It’s like planting a tree expecting **fruit** but then blaming the weather when it doesn’t grow as fast as planned.

Female leaders in the industry might see this as a sign of shifting priorities. Ford’s change of tune shows how quickly business plans can flip when market conditions change. During the pandemic, carmakers were running their **operation** at full capacity because demand was high and money was cheap. Now, with higher costs and fewer buyers, they’re struggling to keep up. It’s a reminder that even big companies can misjudge the future, especially when they **sing** the same tune as everyone else one day and switch the next.

The whole situation highlights how unpredictable the EV market is. Ford’s U-turn isn’t just about jobs—it’s about admitting they didn’t see the slowdown coming. The rules were meant to push progress, but now the industry is asking for a pause. It’s a classic case of wanting the benefits without the challenges.

P.P.S This story is a good example of how policies and businesses don’t always move in sync.
